Let’s take a closer look at Chapter 10—Living Forward: Embracing Regret as a Guide.
As we wrap up this journey through regret, there’s a new way to see things. Regret isn’t something you need to fear, or push away. Actually, it’s more like a companion—a voice that walks with you, nudging you toward a richer, more meaningful life.
Picture a woman in her seventies, looking back on everything she’s done. She feels both proud and regretful. She remembers the choices she made, the risks she dared to take, the relationships she built and cared for. Sure, there are a few things she wishes she’d done differently. But she also sees how those regrets shaped her, taught her, and quietly pointed her in new directions.
Here’s something a lot of people don’t realize: Regret is actually a sign of a life fully lived. Think about it. If you regret something, it means you cared enough to try, to risk, to love. It’s a gentle reminder that life is messy, mistakes are going to happen, and that’s okay. Growth is always possible—no matter where you are on your journey.
Now, imagine a young man just starting out. He feels that pressure to make all the “right” choices. You know that feeling—worried about missing out, or failing, or looking back with regret. But as he listens to stories from those who’ve gone before him, he starts to realize something important. Regret doesn’t have to be the end of his story. In fact, it’s just the beginning—a new chance to learn, to change, and to move forward.
When you face regret with courage and a little compassion for yourself, it transforms. Regret becomes a guide. It shows you what matters most. It points you back to your deepest values, the things that really shape a meaningful life.
So, let regret invite you to forgive yourself. Let it encourage you to reach out, to try again, and to keep moving forward. Because at the end of the day, that’s what living forward is all about.
